newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House approves job-training bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House approves job-training bill.

text.p: The House Friday easily approved legislation folding more than 60 federal job-training and adult-education programmes into three block grants for state officials to administer.

The bill, which passed 343-60, was intended to make it easier for those seeking career training to locate what is available. Local employment-training and job-search services would be centralized for "one-stop" access.
The Clinton administration generally supported the bill but would like to see some changes. Legislation to do that was expected to be introduced in the Senate later this year.
The three new block grants would offer:
-- Job training to the chronically unemployed and workers who lost jobs through big corporate layoffs, or downsizing.
-- Adult education and literacy training for low-income persons to help them land a job.
-- Employment training for "at-risk," low-income youth, including high school dropouts.

"The current federal array of job training programmes inhibits opportunities for millions of Americans. Today we took the first stop in reforming this nation's employment, training and literacy programmes for the 21st century," said Representative Howard McKeon, a California Republican.

Job-training legislation passed the House and Senate in 1996 but died after lawmakers from both chambers were unable to agree on a compromise bill. The legislation was doomed after conservative groups led by Phyllis Schlafly said certain provisions were an attempt by the federal government to grab control of education and the job markets.
Controversial portions of the 1996 legislation were dropped this time around.

While combining most youth job-training programmes into a block grant, the legislation would keep federal control over the Jobs Corp programme providing vocational training to disadvantaged youths aged 16-24.

States would be required to develop benchmarks and goals to evaluate the performance of the block grants. The legislation also would provide incentive grants to states that succeed in boosting literacy and reducing unemployment.
